projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Manuel Martinez was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: Today is December 9, 2003 and I am interviewing Manuel P. Martinez. His birth date is May 30, 1929...1924, oh, I am sorry. And his current address is [address deleted]. What war and branch of service do you serve in?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: The Second World War.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: And what was your rank?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: (inaudible) Private First Class.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: What branch did you serve in?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: The Army and the aircraft artillery.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: Where did you actually serve at?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: I served at... in... England, the invasion at Normandy and right through France, Belgium, uh, Normandy and Austria.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: Were you drafted or did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: I was drafted. I was drafted before my eighteenth birthday.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: And... (inaudible)... I'm sorry.

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: And I was... I was trying to get deferred on account of my mama had already had, had brothers in the service. But I couldn't get deferred 'cause there was a man shortage.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: So they needed you.

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: Yeah, but I got drafted before my eighteenth birthday.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: And where were you living at the time?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: In Montrose, Colorado.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: And did you have a choice in picking the Army?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: No, they just... we went to the induction center in Pueblo and then they... they decided... they decided for us... we didn't decide.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: And do you recall your first days in the service? Any stories or anything?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: No. (inaudible mumbling) had a time getting acquainted with each other. (inaudible) we was sent to Fort Bliss, Texas. for our basic training and most of our training was desert, desert training. So we got our training then (inaudible) about four months and then they sent us to the west coast to California. There we stayed and we thought we was going the Pacific/ But then they put us in a train and shipped us to the east coast and we shipped out from the New York harbor (inaudible) in Boston and uh (inaudible) and from there the took us by truck to New York harbor and shipped out from there. We went to England. We were there for about three months waiting for the invasion. And after, after three months we loaded up we got alerted for the invasion, which was in 1944- June 6, 1944. We landed on a beachhead six plus, six days after. It was still. I'll tell you it was still like going in the beach (inaudible) still there was all kinds of bodies laying on the beach both German and American bodies. From there, we were in Saint Lowell for about three weeks and then we moved up to ( I can't think of the name of ) another city. There we set up on the field. (Inaudible) we don't remember. We used to eat with a French family; we shared our rations with them. And from there we kept going we went to Belgium. And in Belgium we set up at Liège that's the name of a town. We stayed there 'til the breakthrough in Bastogne. Did you hear of that?

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: Ummh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: We were right out... right there. (Inaudible) One night after the breakthrough they were sending paratroopers over (inaudible mumbling) ranges. They were dropping them on that airfield we was protecting. (Mumbling inaudible) We was, we was (inaudible) so they had us... load our, load our equipment (inaudible mumbling) dynamite and stuff to blow it up in case they took us over.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: Ok.

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: But uh they didn't. All the time we were there in Liège they kept sending them buzz bombs over.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: Ummh.

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: You know, we threw rockets.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: Uh huh.

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: And uh, you'd hear them coming lower and see the flash. And when then things cut off they'd come straight down. So... as long as they went lower we were ok. That's all we sweated out that motor keep going. After that you know we, we was there when the war ended you know (inaudible) in Liège (inaudible) from there we went to Munich. You have heard of Munich huh?

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: Uh huh.

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: That's where the Nazi party started. We were there in occupation for... about six months. From there they sent us to Lienz, Austria. That's where the Blue Danube divided the occupation forces. One side was Russian and the other side was where we were. We were allowing them Russians to come over (inaudible).

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: Uh huh.

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: If one of us go over he never come back. (Inaudible) and after that we went back to Munich. From there they shipped us to Nuremburg till we returned home. From Nuremburg we boarded a train and shipped us to uh France. That s where we came back from France there (inaudible) southern France I forget the name of the city it was in southern France. From there we came back and we landed in New York. They sent us to Camp Cower, New Jersey, where we stayed for about a week. And then they sent us back to (Denver) Fort Logan, and that's where we got our separation papers in 1945 (inaudible) and that was it.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: Forty Five uh. Were there like many casualties in your unit that you went over with?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: Uh Huh. There was, there was one bomb hit their gun sight and killed one.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: And what was your job, your assignment?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: I was a gunner. (inaudible) mountable 50 (inaudible) gunner on the portable 50 machine gun.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: And were you ever a prisoner of war?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: And were you awarded any medals or citations for your service?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: Just a French Bordiler (sp) that's the highest decoration from the French. And I got a sharp shooter medal. I got the ruptured duck (inaudible) It's a little medal you put on there for discharge. We used to call them ruptured ducks. (Inaudible ringing).

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: This is the end of segment one. This is the beginning of segment two. When you were in World War Two, how did you stay in touch with your family?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: By mail.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: What was the food like over there? Like your rations you talked about.

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: Just rations, C-rations mostly.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: Did you have plenty of supplies?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: Yea. Usually yeah we weren't short on them.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: Did you feel any pressure or stresses while you were over there?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: At times you get homesick.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: Was there something special you did for good luck?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: Just pray a lot.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: How did people entertain themselves?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: They just had the USO shows.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: And there were entertainers I guess?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: Yeah. From here.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: From the States?

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: And what did you do when you were on leave did you ever get to come back... I mean when you came back after '45?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: After '45? I went to work in the railroad.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: Railroad?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: Yeah, then I quit. And then I went to the coalmines. I worked three years in the coal mines. After that I got married... in '49. Then in '51 I reenlisted in the Air Force and they shipped us to Okinawa and we was there eighteen months

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: Eighteen months? What was it like over there? Similar to this experience or different?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: It was different. You had the cave there. They called it the cave of the winds. The Japanese were sending all the young girls (virgins.) Sending them in that cave. They never survived. They called it the cave of the winds. Then they had a cliff too. I saw that suicide cliff and when we were coming (the army) the people was jumping off the cliff (the natives, the Okinawan natives) 'cause the Japanese told them we was going to rape them and all that.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: Scared them huh?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: So you did see combat over there too?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: No, we just set up there.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: And then were there many casualties that time in your unit?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: No. We just set up just in case.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: Did you get to go on leave?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: Over there?

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: And do you recall out of both of your experiences um any particularly humorous or unusual events?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: (Inaudible) just daily life... just routine.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: And then were there any pranks played you know on other um soldiers just kinda messin' around?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: Everybody was...

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: Pretty serious?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: Yeah. Some wasn't coming back.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: (surprised nervous laugh) Do you have photographs?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: Do you still keep in contact with the people that... ?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: No. We were all from different parts of the country.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: What did you think of some of the officers or fellow soldiers you served with?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: They were pretty good, everybody was pretty nice.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: Did you personally keep a diary about what was going on?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: No, just my memory.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: Good memory. (mutual laugh).

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: And then I did some homework on when I was there in Okinawa.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: Did you make any close friendships while you were in the service?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: Yeah lot of them after we got discharged that was it.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: That was it?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: Did you join a veteran's organization?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: I know you told me kind of what you did a little bit after you got back from World War Two. You reenlisted and went to Korea, the Korean War?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: Worked in the coal mines too.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: After you came back from Korea?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: No. That was after the Second World War.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: Ok, after the Second World War.

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: Yeah, I reenlisted in '51.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: So, what did you when you got back from the Korean War?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: Okinawa?

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: Yeah, Okinawa.

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: I went work in the Dana piston factory over here. I worked thirty-one years there.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: Wow. Did your military experience influence your thinking about war or about the military in general?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: Well, I was planning on making it a career. I changed my mind.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: Because of war?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: Oh yeah.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: Do you attend any reunions?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: Not really. Nobody kept in touch.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: How did your service and experiences affect your life?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: It made me grow up... made me grow up and think. Think about my future.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: Is there anything you would like to add that we have not covered in this interview?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: Nothing. I am happy to be alive.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: That's a good thing to have (laughter) right there. Definitely a good thing.

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: Yeah, I'll be 80 in my next birthday in May.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: May the thirtieth I'll be 80.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: Eighty. I know they had a service it was like a commemorative service here in Pueblo.

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: Oh yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: And you attended that?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: No. I attended the one they had two years ago you remember.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: Two years ago?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: Yeah, I was on that.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: And did you receive a medal or anything?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: What was the medal?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: I don't know... I'll show you in just a sec... certificate (inaudible).

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: Oh it was a certificate?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: Yeah, and the man who (inaudible).

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: What was it called?

sp.speaker: Manuel Martinez
sp.p: (Inaudible) leaving room.

sp.speaker: Nick Vigil
sp.p: Oh, I'll ask you in a second. This is the end of segment two.
